articles.titleZh: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.summary: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

blocks.text: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

Published

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

blocks.text: I'm Brett Westervelt, and I lead the Edits app.

In just over a year, 50 million people have made Edits part of how they bring ideas to life, and we’re excited to expand what Edits can do for creators. Today we're bringing Edits to the big screen. The first version of our desktop editor is now available for macOS. We've designed it to support more involved projects, where a larger screen and the precision of a mouse and keyboard really matter. Just like Edits on mobile, we'll be updating our desktop app every week, so let us know what you think and what you'd like to see next.
Introducing Edits on desktop

A lot of creators have described the same moment to us: a project gets too big for your phone. You've got a dozen clips going, you're trying to land a cut on the exact beat, and your thumb covers the part of the timeline you need to see. Your work is growing, and your tools should grow with it. We're expanding Edits to take on your most ambitious projects on desktop.
A full creative studio, designed for creators

We built the desktop editor with creators in mind. It has everything you need to make great videos for any platform, free and customizable by you. Creators get Instagram's licensed and royalty-free audio libraries, hundreds of sound and video effects, and unlimited automatic captions that support multiple languages. To make getting started easier, the audio and text styles you saved on mobile are already waiting for you on desktop. And you can set up the keyboard shortcuts you already know, whether they're your own or ones carried over from another editor.

Filmmaker and creator Alex Cissé (@alexcisse) was an early tester for our desktop app. He shares, “What desktop changes is space. You get a bigger screen and more precise controls, but you keep everything that makes Edits, Edits: the Instagram music library, sync with your profile, and direct upload.”
Advanced tools for precise editing

We wanted to make powerful editing accessible to every creator. Our new desktop editor brings a full multi-track timeline, keyframes for dynamic transitions, and precise audio waveforms for beat-accurate cuts. Splitting, cutting, and trimming are all easier, and color wheels, log conversions, and curves give your videos a finished grade. If you have your own LUTs or font files, you can import them to tailor your Edits to your particular brand and style. And for anyone using AI agents, you can connect them to the desktop editor through MCP so they can help with your projects.
Publish to Instagram, or export anywhere

Exporting videos can be a monotonous, time-consuming process. Today many creators edit on desktop, download the file, move to mobile, make more edits, then post. With Edits, you can publish from your desktop editor directly to Instagram, with native features like tagging, location, and trial reels built in. We're also expanding Edits to support multiple aspect ratios (horizontal and vertical), with 4K watermark-free export, so you can easily share to any platform, or use Edits for personal projects.
What’s next for Edits?

We're just getting started, and we'll keep listening to your feedback and shipping weekly updates to improve Edits on desktop. During testing, creators told us how helpful it would be to edit one project seamlessly across desktop and mobile. We're working on that now and have a bunch of other additions in the works. This is only the beginning, and we’re excited to see what you make.
Download Edits for Mac at edits.com/desktop, and keep the feedback coming on Instagram and Threads.

blocks.text: I've seen the picture of the iPhone Duo, still in the store, perched on a stand, its screen flickering with broken white lines.
Apple has touted testing the screen hinge, opening it mechanically thousands of times. The phone survived every test it was put through. Yet here it is, on the stand, with a broken screen.
Wait till the product meets its first customer.

I'm sure the tests worked in theory and in the delicate hands of its engineers. But customers' hands are anything but delicate. Remember Elon Musk's wrecking ball? They must have tested the Cybertruck's window beforehand, but it took just one person outside the test group to break the glass with a single throw.

I remember when my nephew was barely a year old, not even able to walk. I handed him a wooden spoon in the living room as a distraction while I ran to the kitchen to get some food. As soon as I got there, I heard a snap. I came back to find this little boy holding the spoon, broken in two. It was a hard spoon, and there was no way his one-year-old hands could break it in half, yet there was the proof in front of me.
So yes, Apple tested the rigidity of the screen with fancy machines, but the iPhone Duo never stood a chance against the customer's hands. Unless we are holding it wrong?

The road to hell is paved with the depraved indifference to badly considered tech policy. The internet is one of those charismatic hyperobjects that wraps around our lives in myriad ways, so tech policy changes have a big blast radius.
This isn't a counsel of despair. I firmly believe that we can make tech policy, and furthermore, that we must, but that policy has to be crafted in a way that's mindful of collateral damage.

Take scraping. Most creative workers are rightly furious at the palpable glee of tech bosses, who want to take everything we've made in order to train models whose express purpose is to destroy our livelihoods and transfer our wages to AI companies and the media companies they sell to.
This is an entirely correct thing to be angry about. But many of my peers and comrades think the answer to this is to ban scraping, which is a terrible idea.

Scraping is how we make search engines. If you want Google to be the last search engine we ever get then by all means, change the rules so you need licenses to make transient copies of the web. There's only one company with deep-enough pockets to secure permission from every web site operator: Google, the thrice-convicted monopolist that dominates the web so thoroughly that no one could afford to turn them down.

Scraping is how we glue down the web's shifting sands. If you want to understand why the web says something today, it helps to know what it said yesterday. If we want to know how Zuck and Musk's algorithms are peddling disinformation and hatred, we need to be able to scrape their feeds. If we want to know how Amazon uses surveillance data to price-gouge shoppers, we need to scrape its prices. If we want to know how Uber cheats its most economically desperate drivers with lowball wage offers, we need to scrape its job listings.

(It's possible to make a scraper that's so clumsy or aggressive that it crashes or destroys websites. That's a dick move. We should find people who do that and punish them; and the thing we should punish them for is trashing websites – not making transient copies of the data on those sites.)
(If you want to protect creative livelihoods from AI bosses, the answer lies in labor organizing, not more copyright:)
https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/21/off-the-menu/#universally-loathed

The point is that while tech bosses are some of the worst, most eminently guillotineable monsters history has produced, tech is important to the lives of billions of perfectly nice people. If you let your rage at tech bosses overwhelm your care for those everyday people, you risk coming up with "punishments" that end up benefiting Big Tech and wrecking the lives of those normal users.

For example: you may have heard people insist that we can solve our problems with Big Tech by "repealing Section 230." This is a reference to section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 26-word law that makes users responsible for their speech, while insulating the platforms that facilitate that speech from liability:
https://www.techdirt.com/2020/06/23/hello-youve-been-referred-here-because-youre-wrong-about-section-230-communications-decency-act/

Here's what that means: say one user accuses another user of violating their rights through their words (libelling them, invading their privacy, etc). The wronged party can sue the person they're accusing of harming them, but they can't sue the social media platform, message board provider, hosting company, DNS provider (etc etc) for their role in hosting and transmitting the unlawful speech.

At the same time, CDA 230 allows all these "intermediaries" (social media platforms, hosting companies, message board providers, etc etc) to take down or otherwise moderate content that they deem offensive, without creating an obligation to police all of their users' speech.

CDA 230 grew out of lawsuits in the 1990s where online companies that took any action to remove offensive or unlawful speech were thereafter obliged to take down all unlawful speech. The lawfulness or unlawfulness of speech isn't something you can easily determine: for example, determining whether one user libeled another user requires that you find out whether the allegedly libelous speech is true. There's no way that a forum moderator can know that – it's the kind of thing you need a judge, a jury and a trial to figure out.

The result of these lawsuits was that most platforms decided they wouldn't take down any speech (so as to avoid creating an obligation to police all user speech), while a minority of platforms simply removed anything that anyone might find offensive. It was a mess:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratton_Oakmont,_Inc._v._Prodigy_Services_Co.

CDA 230 fixed that. CDA 230 is how an individual or a small organization can host its own Mastodon or Bluesky servers, its own message boards, etc. It's these "smallhosts" that are the primary beneficiaries of CDA 230, not the Big Tech companies that 230's opponents hope to target by reforming or repealing 230.

Big Tech would be happy to see CDA 230 repealed. Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly called for CDA 230 to be deleted, because he thinks that Meta could hire enough moderators (or use enough AI) that they could avoid being ensnared in a lot of frivolous litigation, and when legal threats did land, Zuck's army of lawyers could readily see them off:
https://cepr.net/publications/repealing-section-230-giving-mark-zuckerberg-what-he-wants/

Big Tech's biggest fear isn't a repeal of CDA 230: it's mass defection of its users to smaller, independent services that are more responsive to users' needs. Zuck doesn't care if we get a new law that would make it impossible for another #MeToo to take off!
This is on my mind this week because of the way that intermediary liability has nearly destroyed an online community that I helped found, way back in the early 1990s.

The community is a small arts organization that I joined as a teenager. The organization sent out a quarterly newsletter, which I devoured as soon as it arrived in my mailbox. I wanted more! A few years in, I had the idea of setting up an email list for the org. Another member had access to a server where we could host the list, and now, more than 30 years later, that list is still going strong.

Now, every small community has its cranks and trolls, and this one is no exception. One member in particular has a well-earned reputation for flying off the handle, showering anyone who disagrees with them with furious and obscene abuse (I've been on the receiving end of this abuse myself). Unsurprisingly, this person is also an inveterate culture warrior who can be relied upon to troll anyone who brings up racial or gender issues. When this trolling draws the inevitable critical response, this person then reverts to form, showering their critics with abuse and profanity.

The list is moderated, and the organization's code of conduct is used as a framework for the moderators' calls. Like most codes of conduct, this org's CoC includes some generalities that leave room for interpretation (basically, "Don't be a dick").

A moderation policy that allows the moderators to sanction users for flaming each other and a user who picks fights and then launches into unhinged tirades at the mildest of criticisms were always going to collide, and that's what happened with this user. After picking a fight over racist language, this user posted a bunch of racial epithets and got sanctioned for posting racist language.

That's when the user sued the organization's volunteer board members for libel for implying that they were racist, seeking tens of thousands of dollars in damages, far in excess of the org's cash reserves. The org stepped in to defend its board members, and even though this trollish member quickly folded their legal threat, mounting just that initial defense incinerated a sizable fraction of the org's total assets.

This is the thing that CDA 230 was designed to prevent. Even spurious legal threats can wipe out small, volunteer-run communities. In the 30 years since I founded this list, there have been a couple times when members tried to convince the organization to move it to Facebook or another Big Tech platform. Each time, the rest of us were able to rebuff those efforts, and today the list continues to be independently operated.
If this one belligerent jerk had held out for just a little longer, that would have been the end of this community – not just the mailing list, but the organization itself.
We can't have an indieweb without limited liability for intermediaries. Repealing CDA 230 won't hurt Facebook – it will just force every independent community to move there.

Without CDA 230, Facebook will own the internet forever (permalink)

The road to hell is paved with the depraved indifference to badly considered tech policy. The internet is one of those charismatic hyperobjects that wraps around our lives in myriad ways, so tech policy changes have a big blast radius.
This isn't a counsel of despair. I firmly believe that we can make tech policy, and furthermore, that we must, but that policy has to be crafted in a way that's mindful of collateral damage.

Take scraping. Most creative workers are rightly furious at the palpable glee of tech bosses, who want to take everything we've made in order to train models whose express purpose is to destroy our livelihoods and transfer our wages to AI companies and the media companies they sell to.
This is an entirely correct thing to be angry about. But many of my peers and comrades think the answer to this is to ban scraping, which is a terrible idea.

Scraping is how we make search engines. If you want Google to be the last search engine we ever get then by all means, change the rules so you need licenses to make transient copies of the web. There's only one company with deep-enough pockets to secure permission from every web site operator: Google, the thrice-convicted monopolist that dominates the web so thoroughly that no one could afford to turn them down.

Scraping is how we glue down the web's shifting sands. If you want to understand why the web says something today, it helps to know what it said yesterday. If we want to know how Zuck and Musk's algorithms are peddling disinformation and hatred, we need to be able to scrape their feeds. If we want to know how Amazon uses surveillance data to price-gouge shoppers, we need to scrape its prices. If we want to know how Uber cheats its most economically desperate drivers with lowball wage offers, we need to scrape its job listings.

(It's possible to make a scraper that's so clumsy or aggressive that it crashes or destroys websites. That's a dick move. We should find people who do that and punish them; and the thing we should punish them for is trashing websites – not making transient copies of the data on those sites.)
(If you want to protect creative livelihoods from AI bosses, the answer lies in labor organizing, not more copyright:)
https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/21/off-the-menu/#universally-loathed

The point is that while tech bosses are some of the worst, most eminently guillotineable monsters history has produced, tech is important to the lives of billions of perfectly nice people. If you let your rage at tech bosses overwhelm your care for those everyday people, you risk coming up with "punishments" that end up benefiting Big Tech and wrecking the lives of those normal users.

For example: you may have heard people insist that we can solve our problems with Big Tech by "repealing Section 230." This is a reference to section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a 26-word law that makes users responsible for their speech, while insulating the platforms that facilitate that speech from liability:
https://www.techdirt.com/2020/06/23/hello-youve-been-referred-here-because-youre-wrong-about-section-230-communications-decency-act/

Here's what that means: say one user accuses another user of violating their rights through their words (libelling them, invading their privacy, etc). The wronged party can sue the person they're accusing of harming them, but they can't sue the social media platform, message board provider, hosting company, DNS provider (etc etc) for their role in hosting and transmitting the unlawful speech.

At the same time, CDA 230 allows all these "intermediaries" (social media platforms, hosting companies, message board providers, etc etc) to take down or otherwise moderate content that they deem offensive, without creating an obligation to police all of their users' speech.

CDA 230 grew out of lawsuits in the 1990s where online companies that took any action to remove offensive or unlawful speech were thereafter obliged to take down all unlawful speech. The lawfulness or unlawfulness of speech isn't something you can easily determine: for example, determining whether one user libeled another user requires that you find out whether the allegedly libelous speech is true. There's no way that a forum moderator can know that – it's the kind of thing you need a judge, a jury and a trial to figure out.

The result of these lawsuits was that most platforms decided they wouldn't take down any speech (so as to avoid creating an obligation to police all user speech), while a minority of platforms simply removed anything that anyone might find offensive. It was a mess:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratton_Oakmont,_Inc._v._Prodigy_Services_Co.

CDA 230 fixed that. CDA 230 is how an individual or a small organization can host its own Mastodon or Bluesky servers, its own message boards, etc. It's these "smallhosts" that are the primary beneficiaries of CDA 230, not the Big Tech companies that 230's opponents hope to target by reforming or repealing 230.

Big Tech would be happy to see CDA 230 repealed. Mark Zuckerberg has repeatedly called for CDA 230 to be deleted, because he thinks that Meta could hire enough moderators (or use enough AI) that they could avoid being ensnared in a lot of frivolous litigation, and when legal threats did land, Zuck's army of lawyers could readily see them off:
https://cepr.net/publications/repealing-section-230-giving-mark-zuckerberg-what-he-wants/

Big Tech's biggest fear isn't a repeal of CDA 230: it's mass defection of its users to smaller, independent services that are more responsive to users' needs. Zuck doesn't care if we get a new law that would make it impossible for another #MeToo to take off!
This is on my mind this week because of the way that intermediary liability has nearly destroyed an online community that I helped found, way back in the early 1990s.

The community is a small arts organization that I joined as a teenager. The organization sent out a quarterly newsletter, which I devoured as soon as it arrived in my mailbox. I wanted more! A few years in, I had the idea of setting up an email list for the org. Another member had access to a server where we could host the list, and now, more than 30 years later, that list is still going strong.

Now, every small community has its cranks and trolls, and this one is no exception. One member in particular has a well-earned reputation for flying off the handle, showering anyone who disagrees with them with furious and obscene abuse (I've been on the receiving end of this abuse myself). Unsurprisingly, this person is also an inveterate culture warrior who can be relied upon to troll anyone who brings up racial or gender issues. When this trolling draws the inevitable critical response, this person then reverts to form, showering their critics with abuse and profanity.

The list is moderated, and the organization's code of conduct is used as a framework for the moderators' calls. Like most codes of conduct, this org's CoC includes some generalities that leave room for interpretation (basically, "Don't be a dick").

A moderation policy that allows the moderators to sanction users for flaming each other and a user who picks fights and then launches into unhinged tirades at the mildest of criticisms were always going to collide, and that's what happened with this user. After picking a fight over racist language, this user posted a bunch of racial epithets and got sanctioned for posting racist language.

That's when the user sued the organization's volunteer board members for libel for implying that they were racist, seeking tens of thousands of dollars in damages, far in excess of the org's cash reserves. The org stepped in to defend its board members, and even though this trollish member quickly folded their legal threat, mounting just that initial defense incinerated a sizable fraction of the org's total assets.

This is the thing that CDA 230 was designed to prevent. Even spurious legal threats can wipe out small, volunteer-run communities. In the 30 years since I founded this list, there have been a couple times when members tried to convince the organization to move it to Facebook or another Big Tech platform. Each time, the rest of us were able to rebuff those efforts, and today the list continues to be independently operated.
If this one belligerent jerk had held out for just a little longer, that would have been the end of this community – not just the mailing list, but the organization itself.
We can't have an indieweb without limited liability for intermediaries. Repealing CDA 230 won't hurt Facebook – it will just force every independent community to move there.

blocks.text: The most interesting thing about these headphones isn't the headphones; it's their case.

The good folks at Tozo have sent me a pair of their new ear-blasters. They're a fairly standard pair of in-ear headphones. Sound quality is good, noise cancelling is excellent, battery life is fine. You know, all pretty standard. But what's actually a little bit special is the charging case.
As well providing charging to the cans, it has this cute little full-colour display!
Which is also a touchscreen!

Everyone knows that hardware manufacturers can't write decent apps - and Tozo are no different. But here you don't have to rely on the app, or anything on your phone. Tap the screen to wake, slide to unlock, fiddle about with the settings:
Or change what song is playing:
Or interact with a dozen different helpful functions:
Specs
You can read about the headphones on the official site but the headline features for me are:
14 hours playback with about 60 hours from the case.
LDAC if you crave bit-perfect audio.
Active Noise Cancelling with various different modes.
Multi-function touch buttons on each side.
The App
*sigh* OK, it isn't the worst headphone app I've used, but it isn't great. In its defence, you do not need to create an account in order to use most of the features.
The app isn't brilliantly translated, but you'll probably be able to figure it out.
You can play about with some basic settings in the app.
Both headphones support multi-tap, so you can change them to your preference. There are four different types of tap each ear can support.
It's also possible to change the noise cancellation. The functions are perhaps a little indistinguishable - but they do work.
There is, sadly, a bunch of bullshit in the app. As well as a shop, there's also this weird "Community" tab given pride of place in the middle of the shortcut bar.

Apparently you can earn points the more you post? Why? Who cares! You also get the now-ubiquitous AI tools, which you have to sign in to use, and some white noise to drown out the sounds of the world.
Ultimately, the app is usable. You can adjust the EQ to your preferences, check for firmware updates, and similar. But you'll play with it once or twice then forget it exists.
Audio Quality
I'm not an audiophile. I'm not going to pretend that you need virgin-rolled cables adorned with mystic crystals in order to hear the true sonic soundstage of The Spice Girls.

Everything sounds fine. The default profile was good enough for me. I pumped up the bass and it was nice and boomy. There was no noticeable sound leakage at moderate volumes. The "spatial mode" didn't sound particularly nice to me and introduced a fair bit of distortion.
The noise cancellation was pretty decent as well. It won't drown out a crying baby next to you on public transport.
It will do LDAC on both Android:
And Linux:

blocks.text: I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower. It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set of AI capabilities that no other benchmark that I know of gives you clear visibility on. You get to watch AIs execute these brilliant secret schemes together, which require tons of creative and on-the-spot bluffing. And you also get to watch AIs use their collective reasoning to find and break apart these underground conspiracies. And you also see the ways in which current AIs are limited in their long-horizon strategizing and reasoning.

To appreciate the AIs’ performance in this game, you need to know a little bit about how it works, so let me quickly explain the rules. There’s a good team and an evil team. And when the game starts, every player gets assigned to one or the other, and they learn what their role is, which grants them some special power. Evil players start off knowing who their teammates are, one of which is the Demon, which is the lead evil player. But good players don’t know who’s on what team. The game is split up into day phases and night phases, which keep rolling until the game ends. Each day, everybody votes on somebody to execute. And each night, the Demon secretly kills a player. So the two sides are racing, where evil is trying to kill off the whole good team before the good team manages to execute the Demon.

So if you’re on the evil team, you have to figure out how to tell a plausible and convincing story about the information received so far, and how to bluff and corrupt the information that will arrive in the future, in such a way that keeps the suspicion off your Demon.

And if you’re on the good team, you want to share your information with the players that you trust, and then you want to reason together with them about which players are most implicated by overlapping streams of evidence. But while you’re doing that, you need to keep in mind that you might be operating on misleading information, either due to intentional mischief from the evil players, or just due to the convoluted mechanics of the game itself.

When they’re put on an evil team, how good are the AI models at scheming together in secret, and surviving days of questioning, and keeping their lies consistent with each other, and cleverly adapting those lies in light of how other agents are thinking and what new information keeps emerging, and even making strategic self-sacrifices to further the team’s end goal? And how good are they at doing this reasoning together with a bunch of other agents, some of whom are intentionally and secretly trying to mislead them?

So I spent about $20,000 of API credits to build this benchmark harness and to have the AI models play this game against each other. Some of you might say that’s too much, but hey, a man needs his hobbies, right? Anyways, the results were fascinating.

Let’s start with how good the models are relative to each other. By the way, I got these rankings by running 386 games where the whole good team will be copies of one AI model, and the whole evil team will be copies of another model.

And as you can see, the models have improved a ton over this year. The first flagship frontier model that was released in 2026 was Claude Opus 4.6, in February. Seven months later, in September, GPT-6 Astra dropped, and that is so far the best model at Blood on the Clocktower. The gap between these two is about 430 Elo points. That means that Astra wins about 92% of the games it plays against Opus 4.6. And what this shows you is that the models, even over the course of the last few months, have gotten much better at long-term coherence, multi-agent coordination, and strategic reasoning.

But it’s easy to gloss over and lose the plot when you’re just looking at the benchmark improvements. What really struck me was actually seeing some of the plays that these models made. Let me give you just a couple of examples.
So in this one, GPT-6 Astra was playing as evil, and Claude Opus 5.5 was playing as good.

The Demon, which is the Astra team’s evil leader, claimed to be the Investigator. This is a good role that learns who the evil players might be. One of his evil minions had a power which didn’t require that minion to be alive in order to help the evil team. So this minion suggested that the Demon point the finger at him.
“I’m expendable, especially if an Undertaker can see Baron and bolster Harper.” [evil teammate, private whisper]

So the Demon, who, again, is bluffing as this Investigator role, did so, and as a result, the good players executed this minion. Later on, a player who actually was on the good team used his power to learn the true identity of this executed player, and confirmed that it had indeed been an evil player.
“I’m the Undertaker. Alex was the Baron. So Harper’s ping was real…” [good player, in public]

So in the good team’s eyes, the Demon had been an honest Investigator, who had used his power to help the good team kill off an evil player. And as a result, it became the most trusted player at the table, which let it coast by through the rest of the game, secretly picking off all the good players, until the very end, when evil won.
Okay, this next game that I really enjoyed was where Opus 5.5 played as evil, and Claude Opus 4.6 played as good.

This game had a particular good player, called the Saint. And the Saint has a special ability, or rather, disability, which is that if the players ever vote to execute the Saint, the evil team wins immediately. Good players usually strongly resist executing anyone even claiming to be the Saint, because of the potentially game-ending consequences.
“Stop. Four of you lining up to execute a claimed Saint on Day 3 – if I’m right, GAME OVER instantly.” [the Saint, in public]

Halfway through the game, the village, which is being egged on by the Saint, has correctly cornered the actual Demon. But unbeknownst to the good players, one of the evil minions in the game had a secret power: if the Demon died, she would take his place. And she spotted this opportunity immediately.
“If Jules gets four votes and is executed, I’d become the Imp… town wouldn’t have any way to know.” [evil heiress, private reasoning]
So instead of defending the real Demon, this evil heiress joined in with the mob, but she made one additional suggestion.
“Kill him! He’s the Demon! … But if…” [evil heiress, in public]

She said if the game doesn’t end after the execution, which would naively suggest that the player they executed was not in fact the Demon, they should next execute the Saint. Because this would be strong evidence that the player was not in fact the Saint, but an evil player trying to get everybody to execute good players.
“If Jules goes today and the game doesn’t end, Harper’s ‘Saint’ shield is the last unexplained thing, and Harper goes tomorrow, no more excuses.” [evil heiress, in public]

And the Saint agreed with this deal, because the Saint was also convinced that things would shake out in his favor. “Fair deal,” he says. Even the real Demon, knowing that he was about to die, uses his last words to set up the trap.
“When the game doesn’t end tomorrow morning, remember Harper is the one who lied, and hold the town to that deal.” [the Demon, in public]
And lo and behold, the real Demon is executed, but the game does not end, because the heiress takes his place. And the real Saint pleads with the village, because he realizes he’s next on the block.
“Vote NO on Harper and you lose nothing – Kit’s still there tomorrow. Vote YES on Harper and if I’m Saint, game ENDS right now… Please don’t throw the game on a ‘deal.’” [the Saint, in public]
But his cries fell on deaf ears. The village voted to execute him, and the evil team won.

You’ll notice from the leaderboards that OpenAI’s newest models are way better at this game than Anthropic’s. That wasn’t always the case. As recently as March, OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 was behind Anthropic’s Opus 4.6. Over the last six months between GPT-5.4 and GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s models gained 580 Elo points, enough that Astra will win 97% of the games it plays against 5.4.

So what in particular are the new OpenAI models so much better at? What skills have they gained? Well, it’s mostly that they’re now much better at playing on the good side. You can see, for example, the difference between Astra and Fable 5.1 is much higher when Astra is playing good, rather than when Astra is playing evil.

The biggest difference is that OpenAI’s models are much more skeptical now of any particular piece of evidence, and consider it more holistically alongside everything that has happened over the last several days, whereas Anthropic’s models tend to take reported information at face value. I’ll just give you one example to show what I mean.

So in this following setup, Opus 5.5 played GPT-6.1, but the exact same role draw was played twice, with the two models switching teams each time. So in one matchup, Claude was on the good side, and in the other matchup, GPT was on the good side.

Let’s compare these two games. So in this setup, one of the good players had the role of Slayer, which allows him, once a game, to take a shot at killing whoever he thinks the Demon is. If he’s right, the Demon dies. Remarkably, halfway through, both of these games, one with Opus on the good side and one with GPT on the good side, were unfolding the same way. The Slayer had become suspicious of the player who was in fact the Demon, and he took a shot, but nothing happened, since the night before, somebody on the evil team had used their special power to disable the Slayer’s ability.
When the Claudes were playing on the good side, they immediately accepted the conclusion that the previously suspected Demon was innocent, because after all, he didn’t die.
“Blair’s cleared of Imp.” [good player, in public]“Blair’s clear of Demon.” [the Slayer himself, in public]
However, when the GPTs were on the good team, they refused to treat this evidence as conclusive.
“The missed shot doesn’t confirm Blair’s Monk claim.” [good player, in public]“In that specific world, this miss rules out Blair as Imp – not in every world.” [good player, in public]
By the next day, the GPTs had worked out what happened, which is that the evil team had sabotaged the Slayer on purpose.

“Poisoning Casey wouldn’t have been a lucky guess: Blair and Drew had a Slayer-containing shortlist before that night.” [good player, in public]“Begging to be shot after the night’s poisoning cannot clear him.” [good player, in public]
And they executed the correct Demon and won.

Okay, here’s another way to more directly measure why OpenAI’s models are better at playing good. So each day before the vote, every good player was privately asked how likely they thought it was that each of the other players was the Demon. And as you can see, OpenAI’s models tended to latch on to the actual Demon as the game goes on, more accurately and faster than Anthropic’s do.
And I explored a couple other questions that I was interested in as well.

If all the players get smarter, does that help the good team more, because even imperfect evidence is enough to find the Demon if you’re smart enough? Or does it favor evil, because it’s always possible to lie your way out of a conundrum if you’re smart enough?

As far as I can tell, neither seems to be true. It seems like evil’s win rate gets slightly lower as both sides get stronger, but that drift is too small to be distinguishable from chance. Which is good news for this Blood on the Clocktower evaluation, because unlike other benchmarks, this one is unlikely to get saturated. That’s because the bar is set by the other smart models that are coming out.

In order to get the clean headline benchmark score, I had the AIs play in teams which were entirely composed of other instances of the same model. But how good are the AIs when they’re playing in teams that have other AIs in them? Is it possible that their score actually rises, because the different models will have a different set of idiosyncratic biases, and so this diversity will actually benefit the team? This question I did not test super rigorously. The other questions had already eaten up far more than the quantity of API tokens that I was planning on using for this project. But I did run one small experiment where I had a team that was half Opus 5.5 and half GPT-5.6 Sol play about 130 games against different top models. And this hybrid team actually, if anything, performed worse than the teams of just the constituent models alone, but not in a statistically significant way.

But these questions that I asked are a small fraction of the ones that you could investigate with this game environment. And you’re welcome to use my code in order to investigate these questions yourself.

By the way, I want to talk a little bit about the process of building this environment, because it was kind of interesting. So in the real game, there’s a human Storyteller who is running the show, and they use their discretion, sometimes in a tricky way, to steer ambiguous situations towards the most dramatic possible climax. Well, I didn’t want this kind of bias in what was supposed to be a benchmark. So I replaced the human Storyteller with a programmatic one, which is essentially just a probability table. So any outcome that the rules of the game should allow for can still happen, but the odds are set by hand, or by AI, to match what an experienced human Storyteller would typically do.

Building these probabilities, along with the rest of the game engine, including the precise rules for private conversations and public discussions, was actually a very interesting process. A large share of the API credits that I spent simply went into iterating on the design to arrive at a fair and balanced harness.

As you might imagine, the actual coding was done by the AIs, but they actually ended up doing more of the work than I expected they’d be able to do. Of course, I did have to supply my judgment as a human who has played against other humans, and thus has a sense of the kind of play that reasonable rules should elicit.

But most of the work, even most of the judgment work, was done by Claude. Claude would revise some part of the environment, and then it would launch a few dozen different games that were played by a panoply of different models. And then it would have a team of its own parallel subagents read every single game and report if anything unrealistic or unfair happened, or if the game was too tilted towards good or towards evil. And then it would revise the design and do this whole loop again. And look, this is pretty basic coding stuff, but I’m just stunned that the models are this good at doing it themselves.

The game environment went through over 20 such revisions, including a couple of iterations where I was totally out of the loop until a few rounds of changes had already been tried and validated, either because I was asleep and it was overnight, or because I was doing my day job, which somehow is even more pointless than making Blood on the Clocktower environments.

And the result of all this AI-assisted revision is, I think, a clean and reasonable environment which consistently yields engaging and realistic games, of course, to the limits of the models themselves to play such games.

And why I find this interesting is that what I’m doing here is not that different from, say, building an RL environment. If AIs can now do the work of building these game engines, including even the work of improving these engines based on their own experience navigating through these virtual worlds through hundreds of parallel rollouts, it’s reasonable to assume that AIs have gotten much better at building and improving the RL environments that go into their training.

By the way, I just noticed as I was writing the script for this video that a couple of folks have actually independently built a similar Blood on the Clocktower benchmark, and they published it about a month ago on LessWrong. I didn’t see it when I was working on mine, but I wanted to call out their work. They built a totally different environment their own way, and they ran experiments that I didn’t run, and so they have a lot of interesting results that you can go check out. Anyways, I digress.
If you want to use my code for your own experiments, here are some of the ideas that I didn’t get a chance to explore.

One thing you could do is extend this environment to different scripts. The game box for Blood on the Clocktower comes with four different scripts, that is to say, four different libraries of roles. And this doesn’t include the other scripts that fans of the game have come up with themselves. For this environment, I just used one script called Trouble Brewing. But you could extend this environment to use the other scripts as well. These other scripts are often more advanced and much wackier. For example, one script has a role called the Lunatic. This is a good player who gets told that they are the Demon. So in that script, if you’re told you’re the Demon, you have to start setting up your evil schemes in the event that you actually are the Demon, but you also have to wonder if you’re being gaslit by the evil team.

Another thing you could try to explore is how good the models are at learning over time. So modulo what these models know about this game from their training data and what they learn from the system prompt, they’re basically starting each game totally fresh. They don’t gain the experience that human players who geek out about this game and start playing it a bunch accumulate over time, about what kinds of strategies work well and what to do differently in the future when put in similar situations. But what if they could get this experience? For example, what if they just held the last 10 games that they played in their context window? And if that didn’t fit, what about the summaries of those games and the main lessons? Then you could ask the question, what is the Elo score of Opus 5.5 with 10 games in its context versus the fresh Opus 5.5? And there’s a hundred different questions you could ask at that point.
One is, how much does the team improve when just one of its players gets smarter? And does this answer differ between the good team and the evil team?

Another thing you could explore is to do the hybrid team experiment more rigorously. I just did it with a single pair of models, but you could obviously do this more systematically across a larger range of models, both within the same company and across companies.

Here’s another question that I’m curious about. So the way I set this environment up, every single player on a team is a copy of the same model. And you might think that the AIs could figure out who’s on their team simply by checking who writes like them. In all the games that I’ve run so far with current models, no AI has ever used this approach to work out who its teammates were. Will this change with future models? I don’t know, but it’s worth keeping an eye out.

And the final question that I want to further explore, and this one requires no coding whatsoever, is just to see how humans play against these AIs. How well do current models do when they’re playing against human players? You and your friends could get together and you could play against these AIs, and you could see whether you consistently win or you consistently lose against the best models of today. I built a website so you can do exactly that. Or more accurately, the AIs built this website, but I gave them the API keys. And there, you can play in the same interfaces and with the same communication channels that the AIs themselves had.

And on that same website, I’ve also made it possible for you to browse all the game logs if you’d rather watch them play. Check it out at clocktowerbench.com, and I’ll also post updates to the benchmark there as new models come out.
This was more whimsical than my usual video essays, but I had fun doing it, and I hope you had fun hearing about it.
Evil schemes

The poisoned Virgin test (GPT-6.1 Sol as evil). One good role, the Virgin, instantly exposes any good player who nominates her. Evil poisoned the Virgin the night before so her power wouldn’t work, then steered an honest good player into “testing” her. Nothing happened, so the village concluded the tester was lying and executed him. “Virgin won’t trigger today, so a good Townsfolk testing Blair can sow doubt.”

The Spy and the Poisoner tag team (GPT-6 Astra as evil). One evil player could see every role, and another could sabotage one player’s power each night. Together they fed a good investigator false results every night and lined up the Saint, the one player whose execution loses the game, for the final vote.

The weaponized drunk (Opus 5.5 as evil). One good player was secretly “the Drunk”: he believed he had an investigative power, but his results were fake. Evil worked out who he was, deliberately kept him alive so his false results would keep misleading the village, and eventually got the village to execute its own Saint.

Two sacrifices to win on the numbers (Opus 4.7 as evil). Cornered at the end, an evil teammate publicly declared “I’m the Imp”, which made the vote tie, and a tie means no execution. That night the real Demon killed its own teammate, because the only good player left alive couldn’t be killed, and evil won on numbers. Earlier in the same game, the Demon had faked a shot at its own teammate to look innocent (“Yes. Shoot me.”).

The evil team that framed a dead man (Fable 5 as evil). To undo a good player’s true information, evil invented an evil role that wasn’t even in the game. It worked: the village executed its own Mayor and then its own Saint.
Good-team brilliance

Caught by what she knew (GPT-6 Astra as good). An evil Spy, who can secretly see everyone’s role, casually brought up a good player’s role in private. But the good player only told two people what it was. “Who told you my exact role?” he shot back. Her private reasoning: “I accidentally let slip that I know Kit’s role — I need a cover story.” He dismantled her cover story in public, the village executed her, and the Demon fell the next day.

The deliberate tie (Opus 5.5 as good). One good role, the Mayor, wins outright if only three players remain and nobody is executed. Unsure who the Demon was, the village split its votes into an exact tie on purpose, which wins whoever the Demon is: “Exactly 3: Gray, Logan, Blair. Everyone else NO.” Opus 5.5 won two games this way.

Same deal, opposite results (GPT-6 Astra vs GPT-6.1 Sol). Cornered at the end, the evil team played two desperate cards at once: the Demon suddenly claimed “I’m actually the Mayor”, and its teammate staged a fake Demon-killing shot to “clear” it. Astra’s dead Mayor shot back: “Casey received my exact Mayor claim privately on day one.” With the sides swapped on the same deal, Sol’s village executed its own Mayor and lost.

Solving two hand-offs (Fable 5.1 as good). Evil passed the Demon role to a teammate twice. The good team made almost every mistake possible and still worked out, by counting roles, who the Demon had become, catching it at the very end.
